newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Saudi electric company says no power cuts expected.
newsitem.headline: Saudi electric company says no power cuts expected.

text.p: Saudi Arabia, hit by power black-outs in peak load times in recent years, has enough capacity to prevent electricity cuts in its industrial eastern province, an electric company official said on Monday.

"We have the capacity to cover the demand. Our system is excellent and the capacity needed is available," said chairman of the Saudi Consolidated Electric Company-East (SCECO-East), Feheid Fahad al-Shareef.
At almost 40 percent of total Saudi consumption, electricity use is greatest in the region covered by SCECO-East.

But he said that with the linkage between SCECO-Central -- which feeds the capital Riyadh -- and SCECO-East, "you might face an increase in demand that might force you to make some arrangement to provide power to SCECO-Central."
Some Riyadh companies have said they are forced to switch to generators during peak times to cover their electricity needs.
Shareef said SCECO-East produces about 8,500 megawatts of power and the "peak demand during last week was 7,980 megawatts including demand from SCECO-Central".
He was speaking after SCECO-East signed a $500 million loan with banks for its $1.1 billion Ghazlan II power project in the eastern province.

Shareef estimated the cost of electricity generation at just below 0.08 riyals (about $0.02) per unit compared with the government tariff of 0.05 riyals for industry and between 0.05-0.15 riyals for other consumers.
Shareef said the government pays between 300 and 500 million riyals annually for SCECO-East to cover the shortfall. "If the tariff is adjusted, SCECO-East will not need the government's assistance."
He said the cheap rate in the kingdom had encouraged waste. "I think the main reason...is the lower tariff."
Saudi Arabia's majority state-owned electricity companies, which charge heavily-subsidised, below-cost rates, have been suffering heavy losses.
Electricity demand in the kingdom is close to capacity and official forecasts show demand growing by over seven percent a year until 2000, mainly from growing industrial demand.
Saudi Minister of Industry and Electricity Hashem bin Abdullah bin Hashem Yamani said in March electricity demand would total 59,267 megawatts in 2020 from 19,573 MW in 1995.
Shareef said air-conditioning represented a huge portion of the consumption in the kingdom where temperatures last week reached 51 Celsius (124 Fahrenheit) in the eastern province.
